text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average rose sharply Monday as investors sought the relative safety of blue-chip stocks in an increasingly volatile market.
At 1 p.m. EST, the 30-stock Dow Jones was up 43.87 points at 6,975.49 after a gain of 50 points triggered the New York Stock Exchange's curbs on programme trading just after noon.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines by a small margin on volume of about 256 million shares.

"It looks like International Business Machines and Philip Morris are driving the market today. The same concentration you often see in the averages is still in place," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.

"We're having a rebound in some of the techs, though the group still looks tired," he said. "People are moving into consumer non-durables. They feel safer with those stocks and feel they can avoid earnings disappointments. I think the consumer non-durables, not the techs, will be the place to be over the next couple of weeks."
Dow component IBM was among the leaders in the technology group, rising 3-7/8 to 141-1/2. Philip Morris Cos. rose 4-3/4 to 133-3/4 and Merck & Co. was up 2-3/8 to 97-1/2.
The Nasdaq Composite Index -- a barometer of the high technology stocks -- was up 1.83 at 1,336.15.
"This morning you reached something of a climactic bottom in the networking area and the techs," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
Neither bonds nor the broad market echoed the strength in the Dow index.
Analysts said this was due to caution and hesitation ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's two-day congressional testimony starting Wednesday.

"It's not so much an issue of what Greenspan says as how he says it," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "I think he will be circumspect and careful. The market will either be guarded after his testimony or it will get a new lease on life. If I were to guess, I'd guess the market will respond in a guarded manner."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was off 10/32, raising its yield to 6.66 percent from 6.64 percent on Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"The market is on hold, waiting for the Greenspan testimony," Johnson said.
"There are worries Greenspan might make strong statements about speculation in the market and about tightness in labour markets and upward pressure on wages.
"Portfolio managers are on hold. The sense of urgency to put money to work in the market is gone, and that is the overriding tone of the stock market," Johnson said.
